papers.title: Person-to-person transmission of Andes virus: a narrative review of current evidence and its clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses constitute a group of viruses responsible for emerging zoonotic diseases primarily transmitted by rodents. Andes virus (ANDV), endemic to South America, is unique among hantaviruses because of evidence supporting limited person-to-person transmission. The aim of this narrative review is to summarize current evidence regarding interpersonal transmission of ANDV and its clinical and epidemiological implications. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar including epidemiological studies, reviews, and experimental reports. Outbreaks described in Argentina and Chile, together with molecular studies and animal models, support the existence of person-to-person transmission in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly during the early stages of disease. Detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions provides biological plausibility for this phenomenon. The transmissibility of ANDV has relevant implications for patient isolation, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance in endemic regions.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic agents primarily transmitted by rodents, prompting interest in the unique person‑to‑person potential of Andes virus.
analysis.main_directions: The review concentrates on Andes virus (ANDV) as the only hantavirus with documented limited human‑to‑human spread, emphasizing outbreak reports, close‑contact settings, and biological plausibility.
analysis.current_state: Outbreak investigations in Argentina and Chile, together with detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions, provide current evidence supporting limited interpersonal transmission of ANDV.
analysis.gaps: The narrative literature search and the scarcity of quantitative data leave uncertainties about transmission efficiency, risk factors, and the extent of viral shedding.
analysis.future_research: Prospective cohort and contact‑tracing studies, detailed viral shedding kinetics, and evaluation of isolation and surveillance strategies are needed to clarify ANDV transmissibility.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonoses, and Andes virus uniquely shows possible person‑to‑person spread. Main directions: The review examines ANDV transmission, outbreak evidence, close contact risk, and biological plausibility. Current state: Outbreaks in Argentina/Chile and viral RNA in saliva/respiratory secretions support limited human transmission. Gaps: Narrative search and limited data create uncertainty about transmission efficiency and risk factors. Future research: Prospective epidemiologic studies, detailed contact tracing, shedding kinetics, and isolation protocol assessments are required.

papers.title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

analysis.background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens (A1).
analysis.methods: Molecular surveillance was conducted on 1444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites (pooled into 680 host‑associated pools) from 17 sites in South Korea (2022‑2025) using PCR/RT‑PCR, sequencing and phylogenetic analysis (A2‑A4).
analysis.results: Apodemus agrarius comprised 84.9% of captures (A5); Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA was detected in 69.6% of chigger pools, while Bartonella bacilliformis, B. henselae and B. taylorii each appeared in 0.2% of mammal livers (A6); Coxiella burnetii DNA was found in 3.5% of livers, all during autumn 2024 (A7); Orthohantavirus RNA was identified in 2.6% of mammals, predominantly A. agrarius (94.6%) and in 0.4% of chigger pools (A8‑A10).
analysis.contribution: The study provides the first molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in host‑associated chigger mite pools and documents previously unreported DNA of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small‑mammal liver samples in South Korea (A11‑A14).
analysis.limitations: The abstract offers only descriptive baseline data; seasonal patterns, individual‑mite infection prevalence, and vector competence were not established (A15‑A16); only abstract information is available.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Methods: Molecular surveillance of 1444 small mammals and 12,869 chigger mites (680 pools) from 17 South Korean sites (2022‑2025) used PCR/RT‑PCR, sequencing and phylogenetics. Results: Apodemus agrarius made up 84.9% of captures; Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA was in 69.6% of mite pools, while B. bacilliformis, B. henselae and B. taylorii each appeared in 0.2% of mammal livers; Coxiella burnetii DNA was in 3.5% of livers (autumn 2024); Orthohantavirus RNA was in 2.6% of mammals (94.6% A. agrarius) and 0.4% of mite pools. Contribution: First molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in chiggers and first reports of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae DNA in Korean wild small‑mammal livers. Limitations: Only descriptive baseline data; no seasonal, individual‑mite prevalence, or vector competence assessment; abstract‑only evidence.

papers.title_zh: 在韩国野生小型哺乳动物及其相关恙螨中对巴尔通体属、Coxiella burnetii和正汉坦病毒进行分子监测。

analysis_zh.background: 野生小型哺乳动物是多种人畜共患病原体的重要宿主 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在韩国17个地点(2022‐2025)对1444只野生小型哺乳动物及其12,869只附着的恙虫(合并为680个宿主相关池)进行分子监测,采用PCR/RT‐PCR、测序和系统发育分析 (A2‐A4)。
analysis_zh.results: Apodemus agrarius 占捕获总数的84.9% (A5);在恙虫池中检测到 Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA,检出率为69.6%,而 Bartonella bacilliformis、B. henselae 和 B. taylorii 各出现在0.2%的哺乳动物肝脏中 (A6);Coxiella burnetii DNA 在3.5%的肝脏中检出,均发生于2024年秋季 (A7);正汉坦病毒 RNA 在2.6%的哺乳动物中被鉴定,主要为 A. agrarius(94.6%),在0.4%的恙虫池中也检测到 (A8‐A10)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究首次在宿主相关恙虫池中提供了 B. schoenbuchensis 的分子证据,并记录了在韩国野生小型哺乳动物肝样本中此前未报告的 B. bacilliformis 和 B. henselae DNA (A11‐A14)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该摘要仅提供描述性基线数据;未确定季节性模式、单个恙虫感染率及其媒介能力 (A15‐A16);仅有摘要信息可用。

papers.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus– and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

analysis_zh.methods: 对感染三种不同 正汉坦病毒es 的仓鼠田鼠肾脏和呼吸道上皮细胞进行 RNA 测序和转录组分析。

analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究深化了对自然宿主中病毒–宿主相互作用的认识,为监测和潜在防控策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title_zh: 长期局部流行的 安第斯病毒 系列在北巴塔哥尼亚与 M/V Hondius 疫情相关。

analysis_zh.background: 2026年,一起由安第斯病毒引起的汉坦病毒肺综合征疫情在邮轮上发生,凸显了对ANDV传播的担忧 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 回顾性分析将该疫情与2018年阿根廷的事件关联,但提供的证据中未报告具体的研究设计、样本量、地点细节和实验室方法 (A2)。
analysis_zh.results: 调查提示2018年可能存在人传人传播,并在巴塔哥尼亚北部发现一条自2018至2025年持续的单一ANDV谱系,未出现广泛的社区传播 (A3);路径重建显示邮轮首例病例可能在阿根廷暴露,但其时间与预期潜伏期不符 (A4)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究强调需在ANDV流行地区扩大病毒监测,以厘清疫情来源 (A5)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;无法确定邮轮疫情的感染来源,且缺乏方法学细节 (A5)。

papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. Methodology/principal findings A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P Conclusions/significance The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

papers.full_text: Frontiers in Veterinary Science 01 frontiersin.org Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness Muhammad Inam 1* and Hamid Khan 2* 1School of Medicine, Qilu Institute of Technology, Jinan, China, 2Institute of Brain Science and Brain- Inspired Research, Shandong First Medical University and Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences, Jinan, China Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on under­ standing reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they inter­ sect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is estab­ lished. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, work­ load, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively. KEYWORDS Andes virus, hantavirus, occupational exposure, One Health, orthohantavirus, preparedness, rodent reservoir, surveillance 1 Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, three-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses in the family Hantaviridae, order Elliovirales. Rodent-associated orthohantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across much of Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syn­ drome (HCPS) in the Americas (1–3). The transmission cycle brings clinical care into contact with wildlife ecology, occupational health, veterinary practice, and laboratory biosafety. The defining One Health feature of hantavirus epidemiology is that the maintenance cycle operates entirely outside health services. Reservoir abundance and species composition, food availability, rainfall, temperature, land use, agricultural practice, housing quality, waste man­ agement and human behavior together determine whether infected animals contaminate spaces that people use (1, 4, 5). Humans are usually exposed by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or through direct contact with contaminated material. Phiri, Ministry for Primary Industries, New Zealand REVIEWED BY Arif Nur Muhammad Ansori, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Indonesia Yunhui Xiang, Sichuan International Travel and Healthcare Center (Chengdu Customs District Port Clinic), China *CORRESPONDENCE Muhammad Inam 2022390020@gzhmu.edu.cn Hamid Khan hamidkhan193@gmail.com RECEIVED 08 August 2026 REVISED 02 October 2026 ACCEPTED 08 October 2026 PUBLISHED 30 October 2026 CITATION Inam M and Khan H (2026) Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness. Front. Vet. Sci. 13:1962397. doi: 10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 COPYRIGHT © 2026 Inam and Khan. The use, distribution or reproduction in other forums is permitted, provided the original author(s) and the copyright owner(s) are credited and that the original publication in this journal is cited, in accordance with accepted academic practice. No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 02 frontiersin.org Prevention therefore depends on recognizing and modifying ecologi­ cal and occupational interfaces before a patient reaches clinical care. A systematic review of land cover and land use found agricultural land use positively associated with human infection risk in China and Brazil and forest cover positively associated with incidence in Europe, while associations with built-up areas differed in direction between studies (6). Surveillance coverage differs markedly between regions. Some countries have paired human case reporting with reservoir monitor­ ing for decades, while others rely on a few serosurveys or small wild­ life studies, and some have no structured reservoir data at all (7–9). This makes country comparisons difficult: few reported cases may indicate genuinely low transmission, limited diagnostic access, missed cases, or simply insufficient surveillance. A meta-analysis of small mammals across Southeast Asia estimated a pooled hantavirus preva­ lence of 6.07% among 11,806 animals, with the highest estimates in Indonesia and Singapore, in a region where human diagnostic recog­ nition remains limited (8). Work in Cambodia detected orthohanta­ virus RNA in 3.3% of 750 rodents and IgG seropositivity in 10.0% of people sampled at the same sites, with the highest rodent infection rates at urban rather than rural interfaces (9). Attention to these questions has been renewed by the 2026 multi- country Andes virus (ANDV) event linked to an expedition cruise ship, which produced 13 cases and three deaths, contact tracing across more than 30 countries and territories, and a sequence of international notifications before it was declared over in July 2026 (10). The event does not indicate that hantaviruses have become more widespread. It illustrates how a rare zoonosis moving through a mobile and medi­ cally constrained exposure network can rapidly test diagnostic referral pathways and risk communication in settings without endemic transmission. Recent field surveys, systematic reviews, and outbreak reports from 2024 to 2026 have expanded the evidence base on host range, land use, geographic surveillance gaps, and international response (6–10). Yet descriptive One Health reviews seldom specify how a low- capacity setting should move from baseline sampling to an investiga­ tion, or when an enhanced response can safely be reduced (11, 12). This review brings together reservoir biology, exposure, diagnostics, and surveillance to propose explicit, locally adaptable decision steps. The framework is an operational hypothesis, not an established standard. 2 Scope and evidence framing 2.1 Review design and information sources This structured narrative review brings together evidence on hantavirus reservoirs, human exposure, diagnosis, and One Health surveillance. We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. The purpose was to examine evidence relevant to practical surveillance decisions across different epidemiological settings. 2.2 Evidence eligibility and selection Studies were retained when they directly informed one or more areas addressed in this review, including reservoir ecology and host relationships, animal-to-human exposure, human epidemiology, vet­ erinary or occupational risk, diagnostic and genomic methods, envi­ ronmental and land-use influences, surveillance, and preparedness. For specific epidemiological or laboratory statements, we relied mainly on peer-reviewed primary research; systematic and narrative reviews were used to place individual findings in a broader context. We also used guidance and outbreak reports from WHO, CDC, ECDC, and similar public or animal health agencies when these sources provided operational information not available in journal articles. We generally excluded papers devoted only to treatment or molecular mechanisms with no clear relevance to exposure or One Health surveillance, duplicate or substantially overlapping reports, studies with too little methodological detail to interpret, conference abstracts, and non-authoritative web sources. 2.3 Evidence synthesis and framework development Priority was given to primary epidemiological, virological, reser­ voir, genomic, diagnostic and occupational studies, with systematic reviews and authoritative narrative reviews used for broader contex­ tual statements. The synthesis was organized around five recurring questions: which animals maintain infection, where human exposure occurs, which populations are most exposed, how infection can be reliably detected, and how animal, human and environmental infor­ mation can be combined into surveillance and prevention (11, 13, 14). Because the literature considered differed substantially in study design, host species, geographic setting, diagnostic method, surveil­ lance intensity, and reported outcomes, quantitative pooling was not considered appropriate. Findings were synthesized narratively across epidemiological settings, with particular attention to consistency, directness of evidence, methodological clarity, and operational rele­ vance. Greater interpretive weight was given to longitudinal surveil­ lance, well-characterized reservoir studies, linked human-animal investigations, molecularly confirmed outbreaks, and studies with clearly described sampling and diagnostic methods. The tiered sur­ veillance framework was developed from recurring operational needs identified across these evidence domains and should be interpreted as an evidence-informed proposal rather than a formally validated guideline. We considered five dimensions when interpreting a study: rele­ vance to the question; reliable identification of the host and infection; a clear sampling denominator, time frame, and assay; a longitudinal or linked human-animal design when needed to support an inference; and agreement or disagreement with findings from other settings. A serological result without supporting exposure or molecular data was not taken as evidence of current transmission. These considerations informed the narrative synthesis rather than a formal quality score. Table 1 illustrates the kinds of evidence and methodological con­ straints that shaped the proposed surveillance framework. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 03 frontiersin.org 2.4 Terminology and interpretive principles Terminology is used deliberately throughout. Hantavirus refers to the group, while orthohantavirus is used where taxonomic precision is required. We distinguish reservoir hosts, in which infection is per­ sistent and largely asymptomatic, from incidental hosts, and we dis­ tinguish serological evidence of past exposure from molecular detection of viral RNA, reservoir infection from human exposure, and human exposure from confirmed disease. Antibody detection in a rodent or a person is not by itself evidence of current transmission, and a positive rodent does not establish human disease risk in the absence of a plausible exposure pathway. One interpretive principle applies throughout: absence of pub­ lished surveillance is not equivalent to absence of infection. Evidence- sparse settings are therefore discussed in terms of surveillance gaps and preparedness needs rather than assumed local transmission or assumed local safety. The distinction matters particularly for neglected zoonoses, where diagnostic capacity and small-mammal sampling tend to be concentrated in a small number of research centers. 3 Hantavirus biology and disease spectrum The genome comprises small (S), medium (M) and large (L) seg­ ments encoding the nucleocapsid protein, the Gn/Gc glycoprotein precursor and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively (15). Genetic diversity arises through mutation, reassortment, pro­ longed host association and occasional host-switching events (16, 17). full_text_sections.full_text: Frontiers in Veterinary Science 01 frontiersin.org Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness Muhammad Inam 1* and Hamid Khan 2* 1School of Medicine, Qilu Institute of Technology, Jinan, China, 2Institute of Brain Science and Brain- Inspired Research, Shandong First Medical University and Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences, Jinan, China Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on under­ standing reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they inter­ sect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is estab­ lished. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, work­ load, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively. KEYWORDS Andes virus, hantavirus, occupational exposure, One Health, orthohantavirus, preparedness, rodent reservoir, surveillance 1 Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, three-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses in the family Hantaviridae, order Elliovirales. Rodent-associated orthohantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across much of Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syn­ drome (HCPS) in the Americas (1–3). The transmission cycle brings clinical care into contact with wildlife ecology, occupational health, veterinary practice, and laboratory biosafety. The defining One Health feature of hantavirus epidemiology is that the maintenance cycle operates entirely outside health services. Reservoir abundance and species composition, food availability, rainfall, temperature, land use, agricultural practice, housing quality, waste man­ agement and human behavior together determine whether infected animals contaminate spaces that people use (1, 4, 5). Humans are usually exposed by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or through direct contact with contaminated material. A systematic review of land cover and land use found agricultural land use positively associated with human infection risk in China and Brazil and forest cover positively associated with incidence in Europe, while associations with built-up areas differed in direction between studies (6). Surveillance coverage differs markedly between regions. Some countries have paired human case reporting with reservoir monitor­ ing for decades, while others rely on a few serosurveys or small wild­ life studies, and some have no structured reservoir data at all (7–9). This makes country comparisons difficult: few reported cases may indicate genuinely low transmission, limited diagnostic access, missed cases, or simply insufficient surveillance. A meta-analysis of small mammals across Southeast Asia estimated a pooled hantavirus preva­ lence of 6.07% among 11,806 animals, with the highest estimates in Indonesia and Singapore, in a region where human diagnostic recog­ nition remains limited (8). Work in Cambodia detected orthohanta­ virus RNA in 3.3% of 750 rodents and IgG seropositivity in 10.0% of people sampled at the same sites, with the highest rodent infection rates at urban rather than rural interfaces (9). Attention to these questions has been renewed by the 2026 multi- country Andes virus (ANDV) event linked to an expedition cruise ship, which produced 13 cases and three deaths, contact tracing across more than 30 countries and territories, and a sequence of international notifications before it was declared over in July 2026 (10). The event does not indicate that hantaviruses have become more widespread. It illustrates how a rare zoonosis moving through a mobile and medi­ cally constrained exposure network can rapidly test diagnostic referral pathways and risk communication in settings without endemic transmission. Recent field surveys, systematic reviews, and outbreak reports from 2024 to 2026 have expanded the evidence base on host range, land use, geographic surveillance gaps, and international response (6–10). Yet descriptive One Health reviews seldom specify how a low- capacity setting should move from baseline sampling to an investiga­ tion, or when an enhanced response can safely be reduced (11, 12). This review brings together reservoir biology, exposure, diagnostics, and surveillance to propose explicit, locally adaptable decision steps. We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. analysis.background: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting a review of their zoonotic risk.
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes evidence on reservoir ecology, human exposure pathways, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across regions.
analysis.current_state: A three‑tier, risk‑proportionate framework (baseline readiness, enhanced investigation, sustained integrated surveillance) is proposed to guide preparedness where transmission is established.
analysis.gaps: The framework’s triggers, workload requirements, and real‑world impact have not yet been prospectively evaluated, leaving uncertainty about its operational effectiveness.
analysis.future_research: Prospective field evaluations of the tiered surveillance model, including diagnostic capacity and contact‑management strategies highlighted by the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship event, are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses in small mammals cause severe renal and cardiopulmonary syndromes, driving a One Health review. Main directions: The paper integrates reservoir ecology, exposure routes, clinical diagnostics, genomics, and surveillance. Current state: It proposes a three‑tier, risk‑proportionate surveillance framework. Gaps: Triggers, workload, and impact of the framework remain unevaluated. Future research: Prospective testing of the tiered model and diagnostic/contact‑management capacities, as illustrated by the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak, is required.

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. CONCLUSION: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic orthohantavirus disease characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak; atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis, creating diagnostic difficulty.
analysis.methods: The report describes a single patient evaluated with computed tomography (CT) and contrast‑enhanced CT, whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) for pathogen detection, and supportive clinical management.
analysis.results: A 33‑year‑old man presented with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10^9/L), renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria; CT showed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe pancreatitis but only mild pancreatic changes, progressive retroperitoneal exudation, and bilateral pleural effusion; mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (and hepatitis B virus); the patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment, and pre‑discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology.
analysis.contribution: The case highlights that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can clinically and radiologically mimic severe acute pancreatitis, identifies key diagnostic clues (disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, preserved pancreas), and demonstrates that mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation to guide appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: The evidence is limited to an abstract of a single case report; no broader epidemiologic data, long‑term follow‑up, or comparative analysis are provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a zoonotic orthohantavirus disease that can mimic acute pancreatitis, complicating diagnosis. Methods: A single patient underwent CT imaging, contrast‑enhanced CT, and whole‑blood mNGS, with supportive clinical care. Results: The patient had fever, vomiting, diarrhea, severe thrombocytopenia (29 × 10^9/L), renal impairment, and imaging showing retroperitoneal exudation with mild pancreatic changes; mNGS detected high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered fully and ultrasound later showed a normal pancreas. Contribution: The report alerts clinicians that Seoul orthohantavirus can resemble severe pancreatitis, outlines diagnostic clues, and shows mNGS utility for early pathogen confirmation. Limitations: Abstract‑only single‑case report with no broader data or long‑term follow‑up.

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热,HFRS)是一种人畜共患的正汉坦病毒疾病,特征为发热、血小板减少、肾功能受损和毛细血管渗漏;非典型表现可高度模拟急性胰腺炎,导致诊断困难。

analysis_zh.results: 一名33岁男性出现发热、呕吐、腹泻、严重血小板减少(最低值 29 × 10^9/L)、肾功能受损、血尿和蛋白尿;CT显示胰周及肾周渗出,提示重症胰腺炎,但胰腺改变仅轻度,伴有进行性后腹膜渗出及双侧胸腔积液;mNGS 鉴定出高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒(以及乙型肝炎病毒);患者在支持性治疗、静脉免疫球蛋白和对症治疗下完全康复,出院前超声显示胰腺形态正常。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该病例强调首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染在临床和影像学上可模拟重症急性胰腺炎,指出关键诊断线索(血小板下降明显、肾脏受累、胰腺保持正常),并展示 mNGS 能实现早期明确的病原体确认,以指导适当的治疗。

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. METHODS: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. CONCLUSIONS: The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

analysis_zh.background: 本研究旨在评估商业化可用的研究用途实时RT-PCR试剂(PDI0008)在西班牙首次进口安第斯病毒暴发期间的临床性能与定性一致性。
analysis_zh.methods: 十四名因安第斯病毒暴发被遣返的个体接受全血和血清筛查;确诊病例按每72小时一次的频率,前瞻性监测全血、血清、咽拭子、尿液和直肠拭子。样本在BSL-3设施中灭活,RNA自动提取后使用RealStar® 汉坦病毒-HPS RT-PCR试剂检测;所有样本亦在西班牙国家参考实验室使用汉坦病毒-特异性RT-PCR参考方法进行分析,评估定性一致性、Ct相关性和病毒RNA动态。
analysis_zh.contribution: RealStar® 汉坦病毒-HPS RT-PCR试剂与参考方法具有高度定性一致性,并在暴发调查和纵向随访期间提供及时分子信息。全血可能有助于纵向检测安第斯病毒RNA,尽管结果为描述性,未能确立普遍性排泄动力学或感染性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 结果为描述性,未能确立普遍性病毒排泄动力学或感染性;需进一步分析和临床研究以确认试剂性能和临床价值。研究仅限于14名个体,并仅依赖摘要级数据。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 作为加速非洲紧急一体化健康准备的催化剂:加强人-动物-环境接口。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是一种啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,暴露了全球及非洲卫生防备的关键缺口;虽然历史上与亚洲、欧洲和美洲的暴发相关,近期2026年跨国 安第斯病毒 集群显示出流行潜力和罕见的人际传播,且非洲尚未确认大规模本土暴发,但生态适宜性和薄弱的监测提示可能存在漏报。
analysis_zh.methods: 本评论回顾全球防备体系,并将其与非洲的结构性和运营性缺口进行对比,重点关注实验室能力薄弱、监测碎片化以及 One Health 整合不足。
analysis_zh.results: 它指出实施挑战包括资源受限和人力短缺,并强调行为和社会因素——如风险感知、社区参与和信任——是有效疫情响应的关键。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者建议通过实验室投入、人员培训、区域合作以及基于社区的风险沟通,强化 One Health 防备,以提升对新发动物源性疾病的韧性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未报告原始数据或详细分析。
